Kipling writes with rich, musical prose, mixing tale and verse. Each visit teaches how England grew from tribes, legions, and crafts into one land. The book endures as a beloved history in story form, where the past walks and talks beside two children at play.
5780-the-rover-boys-at-school-or-the-cad:
Winfield introduces the Rover Boys at school in this first Putnam Hall adventure, where Dick, Tom, and Sam learn they are bound for boarding school at last. Tom cheers the news to Sam, who fears false hopes, until Tom reports that Uncle Randolph told Aunt Martha he would not keep the boys in the house another week. The brothers head for Putnam Hall as cadets, ready for lessons, drills, and scrapes.

It offers the series formula in its freshest form: three brothers, a strict school, rivals, and pranks that test loyalty. The school setting gives the adventure its shape, with classrooms, dormitories, and playing fields as stages for courage. Young readers who enjoy vintage school stories will find brisk chapters, earnest heroes, and a brotherhood that carries every plot.
5873-farewell:
Honore de Balzac's Farewell, translated by Ellen Marriage and dedicated to Prince Friedrich von Schwarzenberg, opens in a hurry toward dinner. A deputy of the Centre is urged to mend his pace, jump, and keep up, if the party means to sit down to dinner when everyone else does. From that brisk, comic opening, Balzac unfolds a tale of memory, war, and a farewell that echoes far beyond one evening.

Readers meet Balzac's gift for turning a small social scene into a large human drama, with soldiers, marquises, and dinner parties as his stage. The story favors character and irony, letting past wounds surface in present manners. It suits readers of Balzac's shorter fiction, and those who enjoy French realism where a farewell carries the weight of history.
6018-the-journal-of-a-tour-to-the-hebrid:
James Boswell records his tour to the Hebrides with Samuel Johnson, dedicating the journal to Edmond Malone. Boswell insists that authenticity matters above all in history and biography, and he appeals to Johnson's friends to judge from internal evidence whether the many conversations are correctly related.

He recalls General Paoli, who fought to preserve his country's liberties and found asylum in Britain, as a judge of truth in an earlier work. The journal that follows gives talk, travel, and character in close detail. Boswell's portrait of Johnson rests on what was said, heard, and remembered on the road.
6635-a-romance-of-billy-goat-hill:
Alice Hegan Rice, known for Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, sets a Kentucky romance in gay, bursting springtime. A colonel, a doctor, a letter burned on a hearth, a shot in the night, and a plea for pardon all flash past in the picture list. The opening chapter lets spring rush through highways and byways, heedless of frost.

Love, wrong, and forgiveness drive the plot, as folk on Billy-Goat Hill weigh pride against heart. Rice writes with warmth and humor, in a Southern voice that feels lived-in. A Romance of Billy-Goat Hill is a gentle, old-style love story, full of Kentucky color and kind feeling.
6788-wilhelm-tell:
Schiller's Wilhelm Tell, in Theodore Martin's translation, opens with a long cast. Gessler governs Schwytz and Uri. Baron Attinghausen, his nephew Rudenz, Stauffacher, Tell, and Furst join folk of Schwytz, Uri, and Unterwald. Herdsmen, huntsmen, fishermen, and a priest join them, with wives, sons, and a rich heiress, Bertha of Bruneck, in the wings.

From that crowded stage grows the Swiss legend of apple, arrow, tyranny, and freedom. Schiller writes with a dramatist's fire for liberty and home. Wilhelm Tell is a noble, stirring play, still the classic telling of Switzerland's founding myth.
6880-the-coming-of-bill:
Lora Delane Porter, a rich and forceful woman, fills the opening of this novel with her daily drive and her firm grip on her family. Her daughter Ruth stands at the center of the tale, and the two books follow Ruth's plans, her marriage hopes, and the clash between her own will and her mother's designs. Chapter titles point to troubled waters, broken hopes, and a slow path toward peace.

Steve, a second leading figure, meets mischance and exile before he finds a way back, and the later chapters turn on rescue, tangled knots cut loose, and new pastures. Wodehouse shapes the whole as a light tale of love and family power, where pride gives way, bit by bit, to a fairer deal for all.
8662-the-camp-fire-girls-at-sunrise-hill:
Margaret Vandercook opens her Camp Fire Girls series at Sunrise Hill, where Betty Ashton sighs over a book until its leaves quiver in her hand. Chapters follow the voice that calls the girls together, their first meeting, the law of the Camp Fire, work, health. Love, and the guardian who watches over them. Pipes of peace, the rose moon, Nan, Polly, and a surprising camp visit all appear before the summer camp ends.

The novel teaches the Camp Fire ideals of the time: outdoor life, service, friendship, and self-reliance, wrapped in a gentle story of girls learning to keep step together. Suspicion, a disappearance, and a warning add mild mystery. Young readers of the 1910s loved the series for its wholesome adventure. Modern readers will find a period piece about girls' organizations, summer camps, and the virtues adults hoped camp would build.
881-lemorne-versus-huell:
Elizabeth Drew Stoddard wrote this short story, first printed in Harper's New Monthly Magazine in 1863, about two months at Newport that shaped the narrator's fate. She stays with her Aunt Eliza Huell, ordered to the seaside for her health, and finds her aunt troublesome, for ill health is not her only trial.

Stoddard writes with sharp, unsentimental prose about family, money, and the wills of strong women. The tale turns on a clash between the narrator and her aunt, and on the choices that follow. It is a fine example of Stoddard's neglected art, praised by modern readers for its psychological bite.
9322-the-nation-in-a-nutshell:
George Makepeace Towle wrote this rapid outline of American history in 1886, called The Nation in a Nutshell. Contents run from American antiquities and discovery, through colonization, independence, and the Revolution, to Washington, the War of 1812, and the Mexican War. Slavery, Civil War, and the presidents follow in turn.

Later chapters treat material progress, letters, arts, and science, with political changes to close. Towle, known for young people's histories, writes briskly for general readers, in short chapters that move fast. The book remains a handy, old-fashioned survey of the republic's first century.
9614-the-case-of-richard-meynell:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote The Case of Richard Meynell in 1911, a novel of the Church of England and its creeds. Meynell, a clergyman, faces the power of the State Church, which owns cathedrals, crowns kings, and sits in the House of Lords through its bishops. Ward's foreword asks American readers to grasp that church's vast reach, from parish schools to public life. The novel turns on what a priest may believe and still serve.

Meynell's case tests faith, law, and conscience, as church courts and public opinion press him hard. Ward writes with grave care for doctrine and for human cost. A reader gets a serious Edwardian novel of religion and reform, rich in debate and in the fate of a good man caught by his church.
9927-the-bronze-bell:
Louis Joseph Vance's 1909 adventure romance opens with destiny and a babu, a girl and a token, and a hero marooned far from home. The chapters carry him through a goblin night and a red dawn, past masks and faces, toward the court of the Maharana of Khandawar.

Vance sets his tale in India, where a bronze bell, a photograph, and a long day's journey bind love to intrigue. His hero moves between British and Indian worlds, never quite belonging to either. Readers get a colorful, fast-moving romance of the Raj, full of color, danger, and disguise.
a-boy-s-will:
Robert Frost presents his first book of poems with a contents page that glosses each piece in a line. Into My Own opens the volume: the youth is persuaded he will be more himself for having forsworn the world. Ghost House, My November Guest, A Late Walk, Stars, and Storm Fear follow, each with its small summary.

Three parts gather lyrics of New England farms, woods, and weather, written in plain speech with strict forms beneath. A Prayer in Spring, Flower-gathering, and Rose Pogonias show the young poet's eye for small natural facts carrying large feelings. The glosses, likely added for English readers, let a first audience watch a major poet finding his ground.
a-romance-of-billy-goat-hill:
Alice Caldwell Hegan Rice, named on her title page as the author of Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, opens in a Kentucky springtime, gay and irresponsible, bursting through highways and byways. George Weight illustrated the book. Billy-Goat Hill is a poor neighborhood above Louisville, and its people guard their pride as carefully as the rich guard their money.

Thirty-one chapters follow a young woman of the hill, a young doctor, a shooting the illustrations hint at, and letters burned on a hearth. Rice mixes dialect comedy with real pathos, as she did in the Cabbage Patch. The romance tests whether love and forgiveness can cross the line between the hill and the town below.
all-s-well-that-ends-well:
William Shakespeare's comedy, printed here in old spelling, follows Helena, a doctor's daughter of low rank who loves Bertram, the young Count of Rossillon. Bertram wants glory and freedom, not a wife chosen for him. When Helena cures the King of France of a fistula, the King grants her the husband she names.

Bertram accepts the marriage under force, then flees to the wars in Italy and sets hard conditions before he will own her as his wife. Helena follows in secret, aided by a widow and her daughter in Florence. The closing scene tests whether cleverness and patience can turn a forced match into a real one.
b09-luther-bondage-will:
On the Bondage of the Will, from 1525, is Martin Luther's answer to Erasmus, the famed Dutch scholar. Erasmus had defended free will in his Diatribe, and Luther replied at length and without mercy. The Latin work argues that the human will, in matters of salvation, is bound and cannot turn itself to God.

Grace, in Luther's account, must do the whole work, or it is not grace at all. He praised the book in later years as his finest, a rare claim from him. Edward Thomas Vaughan's 1823 English rendering carries the text here. The debate with Erasmus still anchors talks on freedom, fate, and faith.
black-heart-and-white-heart-a-zulu-idyll:
H. Rider Haggard gathered three African tales in this volume of 1900 and explained each in his author's note. The Wizard, the first, tells of a missionary faith that triumphs over savagery and death. Elissa rebuilds the Phoenician city whose ruins stand in Rhodesia and imagines its fall. The title story gives the volume its name.

Black Heart and White Heart is a Zulu idyll of the time of King Cetewayo. Its chapters open at the king's court with the trader Philip Hadden, the black heart of the piece, and move through prophecy, a hunt, and the Doom Pool to the lovers' trials. Haggard calls it a story of the courtship and final union of a pair of Zulu lovers. The book is dedicated to a child who died at Bulawayo in the war of 1896.
camp-david-accords-1978-full:
Egypt and Israel signed the Camp David Accords in 1978 after talks at the American presidential retreat in Maryland. President Anwar Sadat of Egypt and Prime Minister Menachem Begin of Israel reached the deal with President Jimmy Carter mediating. The hosted text gives the two framework agreements in full, with their preamble on peace in the Middle East.

One framework sets a basis for settling the wider Arab-Israeli conflict, resting on United Nations Security Council Resolution 242. It sketches self-rule steps for the West Bank and Gaza. The second framework lays out a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel, with Israel leaving the Sinai. That treaty followed in 1979, the first between Israel and an Arab state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-st-g:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Gall describes one of Europe's chief Benedictine abbeys, in the Swiss canton of St. Gall, thirty miles south-east of Constance. Founded about 613 and named for Gallus, an Irishman and disciple of St. Columbanus, it grew from the cell where Gallus remained in Switzerland after his master went to Italy.

A chapel rose over Gallus' cell, and Charles Martel placed the priest Othmar there as custodian of the relics. Under Othmar a monastery was built, favoured by Charles Martel and Pepin, his son, who count with Othmar as chief founders. Othmar replaced Columbanus' rule with Benedict's and founded St. Gall's famous schools, where arts, letters and sciences flourished and manuscript copying built the great library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-knoll:
Albert Knoll was a Capuchin dogmatic theologian, a teacher of the Church's formal doctrines, born at Bruneck in northern Tyrol in 1796 and dead at Bozen in 1863. Ordained a priest in November 1818, he taught dogmatic theology at the Capuchin house in Meran for twenty-four years. Elected to the senior office of definitor general in 1847, he went to Rome and returned to Bozen in 1853 when his term ended.

While at Rome, Knoll wrote his General and Fundamental Dogmatic Theology, published at Innsbruck in 1852, and followed it with a six-volume Theoretical Dogmatic and Polemical Theology, completed in 1859. The entry praises his brief, exact accounts of ancient and modern heresies and his apt quotations from the Church Fathers. It also praises his handling of grace, free will, and original sin. A two-volume abridgement appeared at Turin in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-mac:
Alexander Macdonell was the first Bishop of Kingston in Ontario, Canada, born at Inchlaggan in Glengarry, Scotland, in July 1760 and dead at Dumfries in January 1840. Educated at Bourblach and at the Scots Colleges in Paris and Valladolid, he was ordained a priest at Valladolid in February 1787. After five years ministering in the Braes of Lochaber, he saw his people evicted in 1792 as their lands became sheep farms.

Macdonell boldly offered to raise his clansmen as a Catholic regiment. The Glengarry Fencible Regiment was formed in 1794, with Macdonell as its chaplain, the first Catholic chaplain in the British Army since the Reformation. He then spent two years negotiating his people's emigration to Canada against powerful opposition, and triumphed. In 1819 he was appointed vicar apostolic of Upper Canada and consecrated Bishop of Rhosina, later becoming the first Bishop of Kingston.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-bell:
The altar bell sits on the credence or elsewhere on the epistle side. The rubrics ring it only at the Sanctus and the elevation of both Species, inviting adoration. This holds even in private chapels. It may also ring at the Domine non sum dignus, before Communion, and at other times by local custom.

When the Blessed Sacrament is exposed, the bell may or may not ring at high Mass. The same holds for a low Mass replacing high Mass at exposition. It does not ring at low Masses in such a church. A low sacristy-door bell signal may sound before Mass. It does not ring at high Mass at another altar than the exposition altar. Nor does it ring at low Masses during a public celebration or choir office nearby. From Maundy Thursday's Gloria to Holy Saturday's Gloria it does not ring. The clapper, or crotalus, signals instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelus-bell:
The Angelus bell accompanied the triple Hail Mary recited in the evening, the origin of the modern Angelus. This bell seemingly belonged to Complin, said at sundown in theory, though in practice it followed Vespers closely. In all but a few cases, the Ave bell was distinct from curfew: the former sounded at the end of Complin, the latter signalled day's close and bed-time.

In places in England and France the curfew bell is still rung, prolonged for a hundred strokes or more. Many bells bear Ave inscriptions: Ave Maria, or, on a Helfta bell of 1234, the full Ave Maria, gratia plena, Dominus tecum. In England Angelus bells were very often dedicated to Saint Gabriel. Early rules show the triple pattern. Wells statutes of 1331 direct three strokes struck three times shortly before curfew. At Lerida in 1308 the bishop directed three peals with intervals after Complin as night fell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arthur-bell:
Arthur Bell, alias Francis, a Franciscan friar and English martyr, was born at Temple-Broughton near Worcester on 13 January 1590 and died at London on 11 December 1643. At eight he lost his father, and his mother entrusted him to her brother Francis Daniel, a wealthy, learned, and pious man. He sent Bell at twenty-four to the English school at St. Omer, whence he went to Spain to finish his studies.

Ordained priest, he took the Franciscan habit at Segovia on 8 August 1618, and after his novitiate was called from Spain to help restore the English province. He was among the earliest members of the Franciscan house at Douai, where he served as guardian and professor of Hebrew. In 1632 he went to Scotland as provincial of the Franciscan province there, but restoration failed, and in 1637 he returned to England, labouring until his arrest in November 1643.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-edwar:
Blessed Edward Powell, priest and martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Wales about 1478, he took his M.A. at Oxford, became Fellow of Oriel in 1495, and doctor of divinity in 1506, styled a most learned man by the university. Rector of Bleadon and holder of many prebends, he was a court preacher in Henry VIII's favour until ordered to answer Luther.

Favour faded when he denounced Henry's marriage to Anne Boleyn and disparaged Latimer at Bristol. Discharged from Salisbury's proctorship in 1534, he was attainted with John Fisher for refusing the oath of succession and jailed in the Tower. Sentence waited until 30 July 1540, when he was hanged, drawn, and quartered at Smithfield beside Protestants burned as heretics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bulla-aurea-g:
The Golden Bull, a basic law of the Holy Roman Empire, takes its name from the golden case holding its seal. Emperor Charles IV signed it at Nuremberg in January 1356 and revised it at Metz that November. It fixed the empire's electoral constitution, ordaining that each emperor be chosen by election, with votes vested in seven electoral princes.

Three church electors, the Archbishops of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne, stood beside four secular electors: Bohemia's king, the Rhine's Count Palatine, Saxony's duke, and Brandenburg's margrave. The Bull defined the electors' joint and separate powers in vacancy and in reign, granting them sovereign rights once reserved to the king. That transfer slowly freed them from the imperial head. It also guarded the empire's peace and curbed the rising free cities, confirming rights already grown by custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-corde:
Charles Cordell was an English missionary priest born in 1720 and dead at Newcastle-on-Tyne in 1791. His parents, Charles Cordell and Hannah Darrell, came of the Scotney Castle and Calehill families in Kent. He was schooled at Dame Alice's School, Fernyhalgh, then at Douai, where he began philosophy in 1739. Ordained a priest, he left college for England in June 1748. He served missions at Arundel, in Yorkshire at Rounday, on the Isle of Man, and finally at Newcastle from 1765 until his death.

In 1778 Saint-Omer's English college offered him its presidency, but he would not accept it. Scholarly and fond of books, he preached with some distinction. He stayed a staunch Jacobite in politics. He published many translations, from the Divine Office for the Laity to lives and letters of Clement XIV. He also wrote one original pamphlet answering a candid sketch of that pope's life and government.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-russe:
An entry on Charles Russell, Baron Russell of Killowen, the Irish lawyer who became the first Catholic Lord Chief Justice of England for centuries. Born at Newry in 1832, he qualified as a solicitor in 1854, then as a barrister in London in 1859, and built a practice famed for cross-examination, business sense, and honesty. His fees rose from thousands a year in the 1860s to 150,000 dollars in his last year of practice.

Russell entered Parliament as a Liberal, served as attorney-general under Gladstone, and championed Home Rule, self-government for Ireland. At the Parnell Commission trial of 1888 he exposed the Times forgeries and gave an eight-day speech for the defence. Knighted after the Bering Sea arbitration of 1893, he became a Lord of Appeal and then Lord Chief Justice in 1894. He died in London in 1900, widely mourned across parties and faiths.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-willi:
An entry on Charles William Russell, the Irish priest and scholar who presided over Maynooth College for over twenty years. Born at Killough, County Down, in 1812, he entered Maynooth in 1826, was ordained in 1835, and taught humanities there. In 1842 Gregory XVI chose him for the Ceylon vicariate apostolic, but he refused that dignity, as he refused later bishoprics.

Russell returned to Maynooth as professor of Church history, translated Leibniz's System of Theology in 1850, and published a Life of Cardinal Mezzofanti in 1858. He became president of Maynooth in 1857. He served on the Historical Manuscripts Commission from 1869, jointly editing the Carte manuscripts' eight-volume report and the Calendar of Irish State Papers under James I. A steady writer for the Dublin Review, he was a close friend of Wiseman and Newman. He died at Dublin in 1880.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Edmond Obrecht's entry follows the Missionaries of Mariannhill, a Trappist-rooted missionary body in Natal. Mariannhill sits near Pinetown, fifteen miles from Durban and fifty-six from Pietermaritzburg. In 1882 Francis Pfanner, then prior of Bosnia's Mariastern monastery, answered Bishop Ricards' invitation and the general chapter's consent. He volunteered to plant a monastery in Cape Colony adapting Trappist rule to missionary life. He had landed at Port Elizabeth with thirty-one companions in July 1880, settling at Dunbrody, named for an old Irish monastery.

Dunbrody failed, and in 1882 Bishop Jolivet's solicitation moved the community to Mariannhill. Pfanner's energy won such success that by 1885 the work outgrew its bounds. Within a few years he founded seven mission stations scattered across Natal, from Transvaal's Ratschitz onward. The general chapter at Cîteaux later regularized the new congregation's standing, separating its missionary Trappists from the older observance while keeping the Mariannhill name and Natal center.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert-tuns:
A biographical entry follows Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of London and later of Durham, born at Hackforth in 1474 and dead at Lambeth in 1559. A scholar in theology, law, Greek, and Hebrew, he graduated in law at Padua and won Archbishop Warham's friendship, becoming his chancellor in 1511. Embassies followed, including Brussels with Thomas More, where he lodged with Erasmus.

Made Bishop of London in 1522 and keeper of the privy seal in 1523, he visited Worms and saw the dangers of Lutheran books. In Henry VIII's divorce case he counselled Queen Katherine but urged her not to appeal to Rome. Translated to Durham in 1530, he held quasi-regal power there. Through troubled years he kept Catholic doctrine, though without the constancy of Fisher and More, and died deprived under Elizabeth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-carrol:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Carroll, brother of Archbishop John Carroll, born at Upper Marlboro, Maryland, in 1733 and dead at Washington in 1829. Overshadowed by his illustrious brother, he was in his time one of Maryland's most influential men. Educated abroad like his brother, he lived as a country gentleman until the Revolution, when Catholic men schooled overseas stood out among neighbours of narrow local schooling.

Carroll served Maryland in the old Colonial Congress from 1780 to 1784, then sat in the Philadelphia convention that framed the United States Constitution in 1787. He and Thomas Fitz-Simons of Pennsylvania were the convention's only Catholics. Back in Maryland his efforts helped secure the Constitution's ratification, and he later served in Congress and as a commissioner for the new federal capital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-o-conn:
A biographical entry traces Daniel O'Connell, Ireland's Liberator, born near Cahirciveen in 1775 and dead at Genoa in 1847. His Kerry family, once great, had suffered under the penal laws, and an uncle in France paid for his schooling at Liege, Saint Omer, and Douai. Called to the Irish Bar in 1798, he saw Catholics still barred from Parliament and high office.

Detesting violence and the French Revolution alike, he built the Catholic Association into a mass movement for emancipation, won in 1829. Later he fought the Union, defended tenant rights, and led the repeal campaign, dying on pilgrimage to Rome. The entry follows his legal skill, his oratory, and his conviction that Catholics who paid taxes should share in making the laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-willia:
A biographical entry follows Daniel William Cahill, lecturer and controversialist, born in Queen's County, Ireland, in 1796 and dead at Boston in 1864. Third son of a civil engineer, he studied at Carlow and Maynooth, excelled in natural philosophy and languages, and was ordained after the Dunboyne course. He taught natural philosophy at Carlow, then ran a school at Seapoint from 1835 to 1841.

Meanwhile he wrote for the press, edited the Dublin Telegraph for a time, and became a famed preacher whose attacks on government and the Established Church spread his name widely. Visiting America in December 1859, he lectured on astronomy and preached across the United States and Canada, raising large sums for Catholic causes. Six feet five inches tall and strikingly handsome, he was buried at Glasnevin after exhumation from Boston.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-o-donn:
Edmund O'Donnell was the first Jesuit put to death by the English government in Ireland, born at Limerick in 1542 and executed at Cork in 1575. His family had held high civic office in Limerick for centuries. He joined the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1561, but ill health sent him to Flanders, and in 1564 he came back to teach in a Limerick school.

Troops broke up the school in 1565, and after a spell at Kilmallock the teachers returned, only to face a royal search in 1568. Ordered out on pain of death, O'Donnell withdrew to Lisbon, then risked a return in 1574 and was seized on landing. Tried for coming back, denying the queen's supremacy, and carrying letters, he was hanged, drawn, and quartered. His name also appears in records as Daniell and Donnelly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-caswal:
Edward Caswall was an Oratorian priest and hymn writer, born at Yately in 1814 and dead at the Birmingham Oratory in 1878. Schooled at Marlborough and Brasenose College, Oxford, he first won notice with a witty student satire, The Art of Pluck, signed Scriblerus Redivivus. Ordained in the Church of England in 1839, he served as curate of Stratford-sub-Castle.

Drawn by Newman and the Tracts for the Times, he resigned and was received into the Catholic Church at Rome in January 1847. His wife, also a Catholic, died of cholera in 1849, and he joined the Oratory in 1850. His Lyra Catholica put all the Breviary and Missal hymns into English verse, and his own poems in The Masque of Mary drew a poem in reply from Newman.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-free-will:
Free will, the question of moral liberty, ranks among the three or four greatest problems in philosophy. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry frames it plainly: can a person truly choose, shaping thoughts and character, or are all acts fixed in advance by past events beyond control? How one answers decides the meaning of duty, merit, remorse, and justice.

The article works through the question in stages, from ancient thought and Christian teaching to Thomist and Molinist theories, the Reformers, and modern philosophy. It weighs proofs and objections, then maps the issue across ethics, theology, metaphysics, and psychology. Readers get a full tour of why free choice still troubles every field that touches human action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-funeral-pall:
The Funeral Pall is the black cloth spread over a coffin during the burial rites, most often marked with a white cross from end to end. The Roman Ritual does not order it for every priest or lay burial, but it does require it for absolution after a requiem when the body is absent. Church law also assumes the pall, barring clerics in vestments from bearing it.

Custom once made pall-bearing an honor, with guests invited to carry the cloth or touch its edge in procession. Costly palls later became sacred vestments, and popes were once buried under altar coverings until abuses ended the practice. English funerals show the splendor well: gold cloths for kings, and three red heraldic palls offered at a Durham bishop's burial in 1316.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-dowdal:
George Dowdall, Archbishop of Armagh, crossed from schism to Rome and back to his own see. Born at Drogheda in 1487, he joined the Crutched Friars and was last prior of Ardee, pensioned at twenty pounds a year when Henry VIII suppressed the house in 1539. The king named him to Armagh in 1543, but the pope withheld recognition, and Dowdall owned Henry as supreme head while denouncing the true primate.

Yet under Edward VI Dowdall led Ireland's Catholic party against Protestantism, and, failing, withdrew in disgust to the Continent. After renouncing the schism he was appointed by the pope in 1553 to the very see he had held schismatically. Through Mary's reign he repaired religion's ravages and held a Drogheda synod in 1554 against priests who had presumed to marry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gustav-bickel:
Cassel Orientalist Gustav Bickell, born in 1838, became one of the leading Semitic scholars of his generation and a Catholic convert through his own research. Teaching Semitic and Indo-Germanic languages at Marburg and Giessen, he found a clear witness to the Immaculate Conception in St. Ephraem's hymns while copying them in London and entered the Church in November 1865.

Ordained at Fulda weeks later, he taught at Münster, defended papal infallibility, and held chairs at Innsbruck from 1874 and Vienna from 1891. His books range from Syriac metre and a Hebrew grammar to editions of Ephraem and Isaac of Antioch. They include a study of the Mass and Passover, a rendering of Kalilag and Damnag, and a late work on Job.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harrowing-of-:
Harrowing of Hell is the Old and Middle English name for Christ's triumphant descent into Hades between Crucifixion and Resurrection, when he freed souls held captive since the world's beginning. The word itself first appears in Aelfric's homilies about the year 1000. The descent already filled poems linked to Caedmon and Cynewulf and the prose homilies and saints' lives of Old England.

Medieval English literature gives the theme its fullest dramatic life. The earliest surviving English religious play treats it, and each of the four great mystery cycles devotes it a scene, with Cornish plays beside them. Details in these versions come largely from the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, known in England from early times and paraphrased in the long poem Cursor Mundi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hell:
Hell, a word kin to hole and hollow from a verb meaning to hide, is treated here under eight heads. They run from its name and place to the eternity and character of its pains. Theologians split the term four ways: hell proper for the damned, the limbo of infants, the limbo of the Fathers closed at Christ's Ascension, and purgatory. This entry covers only hell in the strict sense.

Latin infernus, Greek Hades, and Hebrew sheol all point below the earth. Gehenna, from Jerusalem's valley of Hinnom defiled by Moloch worship, became the New Testament's commonest name for the damned's abode, beside pool of fire, outer darkness, and second death. Scripture's abyss language, the entry argues, favours a real place within the earth over a hell everywhere, with fire and loss of God as its twin pains.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-conwell:
Henry Conwell, second Bishop of Philadelphia, was born at Moneymore, County Derry, in 1745. He was consecrated in London in 1820 at seventy-four, after two other clergy had declined a see troubled by lay trustees at St. Mary's Church. Trained at the Irish College in Paris, he arrived that December to find the brilliant but unruly Reverend William Hogan stationed at St. Mary's without credentials. When Conwell revoked Hogan's faculties, a schism followed that lasted for years.

Seeking peace, Conwell made two errors the account records plainly. He recalled the dismissed Dominican William Vincent Harold as vicar-general, and capitulated to the trustees in 1826 by yielding them control of salaries and a veto over appointments. Rome, displeased at that surrender of episcopal rights, appointed an administrator and forbade his return to the see. Francis Patrick Kenrick arrived as coadjutor in 1830. Conwell lived his last years in seclusion and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-weedall:
Henry Weedall, born in London in 1788 and orphaned young, was educated at Sedgley Park and Oscott and ordained priest at Wolverhampton in 1814. Already a junior master at Oscott, he continued teaching classics there. He became prefect of studies in 1816 and, in effect, president from 1821, taking the office in name when Bishop Walsh left in 1826. Under his rule Oscott progressed notably, and the present college building, two miles from the old, rose between 1826 and 1838.

Appointed Vicar Apostolic of the Northern District in 1840, Weedall went to Rome and got leave to decline the vicariate. He spent years in humbler posts until Bishop Ullathorne made him vicar-general, cathedral dean, and temporal administrator in 1848. In 1852 he became first provost of the new Birmingham Chapter. In 1853 he went back to Oscott in its troubled hour to renew its spirit of piety and discipline, succeeding despite almost continuous ill health until his death in 1859.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holywell:
Holywell is a town in North Wales on a hillside above a valley, where a broad stream from St. Winefride's Well joins the River Dee two miles away. Lead and copper mines once made it flourish, but mining decayed and its commercial glory fled. Today the only draw for visitors is St. Winefride's miraculous well.

For over a thousand years pilgrims have sought the well. Two twelfth-century documents in the British Museum record its history and earliest cures, covering dropsy, paralysis, gout, melancholia, sciatica, cancer, and many other ills, plus deliverance from evil spirits. Pilgrims still came in the sixteenth-century persecutions, and Bishop Goldwell won papal confirmation of indulgences granted by Martin V.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-maccaghw:
Hugh MacCaghwell, also called Cavellus, was an Irish archbishop and theologian, born at Saul in County Down in 1571 and dead in 1626. Schooled first at home and then at a famous school in the Isle of Man, he returned to Ireland and became tutor to the sons of Hugh, Prince of Tyrone. The prince sent him as special messenger to the Spanish court seeking aid for Ulster forces.

At Salamanca, where the court then sat, MacCaghwell frequented the university schools and took doctorates in divinity. Soon after, he gave up worldly greatness for the Franciscan order. His commentaries on Duns Scotus won high repute, and his holiness and learning made him, one writer says, the miracle of his time. Largely through his influence at the Spanish court, the Irish Franciscan College of St. Anthony arose at Louvain, where he later taught.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-o-neill:
Hugh O'Neill, earl of Tyrone, was born in 1550 and died at Rome in 1616. Mathew's youngest son, his parentage doubtful, yet Conn, first earl of Tyrone, recognized him as heir, he was ennobled as Baron of Dungannon. Shane O'Neill contested the arrangement, and in the petty wars that followed both Mathew and his eldest son were killed. Hugh became Baron of Dungannon in 1562.

His youth passed partly in Ireland, partly among English courtiers, where he picked up English ways and grew more English noble than Irish chief in manner. Camden praised his industry, large mind, military knowledge, and profound, dissembling heart, judging him born for great good or ill to his country. The entry follows his shifting alliances, his peerage under Perrot, and his later career as Tyrone's earl.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-tootell:
Hugh Tootell, commonly known as Charles Dodd, was an English historian, born in Lancashire in 1671 or 1672 and dead at Harvington Hall in 1743. He studied at the English College, Douay, and at St. Gregory's Seminary, Paris. Ordained, he came back to England in 1698 as the Molyneux family's chaplain at Mosborough Hall.

In 1711 he returned to the Continent, reportedly witnessing the siege of Douay as a regimental chaplain, and wrote a short history of the English College there, attacking the Jesuits. Father Hunter's reply drew Dodd's Secret Policy of the English Society of Jesus in 1715. From 1718 he gathered material at Douay for his great Church History of England from 1500 to 1688, twenty years in the making at Harvington Hall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-bell:
Priest and martyr James Bell was born at Warrington, Lancashire, probably about 1520. He died on 20 April 1584. What little is known comes from Bridgewater's Concertatio of 1588, drawn from a Douay manuscript later kept in Westminster archives. Challoner added details, as did state papers. Bell studied at Oxford and was ordained priest in Mary's reign. Under Elizabeth he unfortunately conformed to the established Church.

By the Douay account he ministered its bare sacraments for about twenty years in diverse English places. At last conscience deterred him from the cure of souls, and destitution reduced him to seeking a small readership for bare subsistence. To obtain it he approached a patron's wife, a Catholic lady, whose influence turned him back toward the old faith. The entry follows a conforming priest's return to Catholic ministry and martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-campbel:
James Campbell was born at Philadelphia on 1 September 1812 and died there on 27 January 1893. His father was Anthony Campbell, and his grandfather George Campbell came from Fintona, County Tyrone. James was educated at Geraldus Stockdale's private school. He studied law with Robert D. Ingraham and was admitted to the bar on 14 September 1833. The next day he became commissioner of Southwark district. He served until appointed to the board of education.

On 16 April 1840 he offered the resolution that founded Philadelphia's Girls' High School. He served on the education board until 1840, when Governor Porter named him judge of common pleas, orphans' court, and oyer and terminer courts. He held those posts until 1 January 1851, when Pennsylvania judgeships became elective. Nominated for supreme court judge during Know-Nothing and anti-Catholic agitation, he faced a hostile climate. The entry follows a Catholic jurist of Philadelphia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-dowdall:
Martyr James Dowdall, birth date unknown, was executed for his faith at Exeter, England, on 20 September 1600. By Rothe's account he was a Drogheda merchant, trading with England and the Continent. Some authorities, including Challoner, call him a Wexford native. Further confusion comes from another James Dowdall who died a confessor.

In summer 1598, returning from France, his ship was driven by weather onto Devon's coast, where William Bourchier, Earl of Bath, arrested and examined him. Dowdall publicly avowed that he rejected the queen's supremacy and recognized only the Roman pontiff's. The earl sent the examination to Sir Robert Cecil and committed Dowdall to Exeter jail. In prison he was tortured and racked, yet stayed unchanged in his fidelity. The entry presents a merchant whose storm-driven landing led to martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-ryder-r:
Journalist and poet James Ryder Randall was born at Baltimore, Maryland, on 1 January 1839. He died at Augusta, Georgia, on 15 January 1908. As author of Maryland, my Maryland, the Confederacy's famous war song, he is often styled poet laureate of the Lost Cause. He was educated at Georgetown University but did not graduate. He traveled in South America and the West Indies. Returning to America, he took the English literature chair at Poydras College, Pointe-Coupée, Louisiana.

Hearing of the 21 April 1861 attack on federal troops in Baltimore, in which a classmate was wounded, his Southern sympathies flared. During that night, by candlelight, he composed America's most martial poem, as it is often called. It first appeared in the New Orleans Sunday Delta on 26 April 1861. Reaching Baltimore, it was set to the music of Lauriger Horatius. The entry presents a teacher whose overnight verses became a Confederate anthem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-adam-s:
Johann Adam Schall von Bell, a leading Jesuit missionary to China, was born at Cologne in 1591 and died at Peking in 1666. He studied at Rome, joined the Society in 1611, and sailed from Lisbon for China in April 1618, reaching Macao the next year amid a mandarin's persecution.

Penetrating inland only in 1622, Schall worked at Xi'an until Peking summoned him in 1630 to reform the Chinese calendar in place of the late Father Terrentius. Calendar-making, a high affair of state run by a two-hundred-member Board of Mathematics, became the mission's lifeline. Schall's science won the court standing his preaching alone could not.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-baptist-:
John Baptist Purcell was the Irish-born Archbishop of Cincinnati who built the Church across Ohio in the nineteenth century. Born at Mallow in 1800, he was barred from Irish colleges by the penal laws and sailed to America, taught at Baltimore, and entered Mount St. Mary's Seminary at Emmitsburg in 1820. Ordained at Paris in 1826, he returned to teach at Mount St. Mary's and became its president.

Consecrated Bishop of Cincinnati in 1833, he attended the Third Provincial Council of Baltimore the same day. He spent fifty years guiding a diocese that grew from a frontier mission into a great archdiocese. The entry follows his long episcopate through the building of churches, schools, and seminaries, and his care for immigrants. It covers the financial troubles that clouded his final years, ending with his death in Ohio in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-carroll:
John Carroll was the first bishop of the Catholic hierarchy in the United States and first Archbishop of Baltimore. Born at Upper Marlboro, Maryland, in 1735 to an Irish merchant father and a mother educated in France, he studied at the Jesuits' school at Bohemia, then at St. Omer's in French Flanders, and joined the Society of Jesus in 1753, being ordained at Liege in 1769.

When Clement XIV suppressed the Jesuits in 1773, Carroll wrote a vindication of the order and returned to Maryland, where penal laws left no public Catholic church. He built a small frame chapel on his mother's estate and began missionary life in Maryland and Virginia, saying Mass in her house on weekdays. From those modest beginnings he rose to lead an American Church that had to organize itself anew after the Revolution, and he died at Baltimore in 1815.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-caryll:
John Caryll was an English Catholic poet, dramatist, and diplomatist of the Stuart age. Born at West Harting in Sussex in 1625, head of an old Catholic and royalist family, he was educated at the English colleges of St. Omer and Rome. Under Charles II he produced plays and poems above the average in merit, including a translation of Ovid's letter of Briseis to Achilles.

His tragedy The English Princess, or the Death of Richard III, seen by Pepys in 1667 and judged no more than pretty good, played at the Duke of York's Theatre. So did his comedy Sir Solomon Single, modeled on Moliere's School for Wives. Imprisoned in the Tower during the Popish Plot scare of 1679, he later served James II as agent to Pope Innocent XI. He was secretary to Queen Mary of Modena, following the exiled court to Saint-Germain and losing his estate by attainder in 1696.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-martiall:
John Martiall was an English Catholic exile who helped found the English College at Douai. Born in Worcestershire in 1534, he was educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford, graduating in civil law in 1556. He then taught at Winchester until Elizabeth's accession drove him and his master abroad to Louvain.

Moving to Douai, he graduated in divinity in 1567 and was one of six companions who joined Dr. Allen in founding the English College there in 1568, a foundation of great importance for English Catholic affairs. Leaving over the smallness of his allowance, he later gained a canonry at St. Peter's in Lille, installed in 1579, which he enjoyed eighteen years. His Treatise of the Cross of 1564 defended honor paid to the cross and drew a Calvinist reply he answered in 1566.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-cornw:
John of Cornwall was a twelfth-century theologian known for a single certain work against Abelard's doctrine. Living about 1176, he came from St. German's in Cornwall and studied under Peter Lombard and Robert of Melun at Paris, and became a teacher himself. From Lombard he briefly took the view that Christ's humanity was merely the garment clothing the Logos.

Abandoning that doctrine after its condemnation at Tours in 1163, he defended orthodox teaching in his Eulogium to Pope Alexander III, arguing that Christ is truly a man. The preface's reference to William, formerly of Sens, as Archbishop of Reims dates it after 1176. Other works, including an apology on the Incarnation and a treatise on the Mass, are assigned to him without sufficient grounds, and nothing is known of his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-baron-:
Joseph, Baron von Hammer-Purgstall was an Austrian diplomat and Oriental scholar who lived from 1774 to 1856. Born at Graz, he trained in Eastern languages at Vienna's Oriental academy and served as interpreter at Constantinople and in Egypt during the campaign against the French. He rose to Aulic Councillor and, in 1847, president of the new Academy of Sciences.

His output was huge but uneven, since his grasp of Eastern tongues was broad rather than deep and his translations were often faulty. Still, his ten-volume history of the Ottoman Empire and his version of Hafiz, which inspired Goethe's West-Eastern Divan, left a mark on history and on German letters alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-creswe:
Joseph Creswell was an English Jesuit controversialist of the Elizabethan age. Born in London in 1557, he studied at Reims and the Roman College and joined the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1583. He led the English College at Rome after Father Persons and then acted as vice-prefect for English Jesuit interests in Spain.

His writings answered royal proclamations, defended martyrs such as Henry Walpole, and meditated on the Rosary, often under false names. His handling of seminary disputes in Seville and Valladolid drew severe criticism from later historians. Sent to Belgium in 1614, he became rector of Ghent in 1621 and died about 1623.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juliana-morel:
Juliana Morell was a Spanish Dominican nun famed as a child prodigy of learning. Born at Barcelona in 1594, she began Latin, Greek, and Hebrew at four and wrote her father a Latin letter before seven. Her father fled to Lyons over a murder charge, and at twelve she defended theses in ethics and dialectics with highest praise.

At Avignon in 1608, Juliana publicly maintained law theses before a distinguished audience and earned her doctorate. Lope de Vega called her the fourth Grace and tenth Muse. Spurning wealth and marriage, she entered the Dominican convent of Sainte-Praxède that year, took vows in 1610, and served three terms as prioress before her death in 1653.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-zell:
Karl Zell (1793-1873) spent his working life in the German state of Baden, first as a classical scholar and teacher, then as a politician who fought publicly for Catholic interests. This reference entry follows him from school in Mannheim through university study at Heidelberg, Gottingen, and Breslau to teaching posts at Rastatt, Freiburg, and Heidelberg.

In the Baden diet he pushed a full overhaul of secondary schooling and helped run the new board that oversaw higher study. Later, almost alone among public men, he spoke and wrote for the Church, Christian schools, and religious orders during bitter clashes with liberal governments. He also advised the Freiburg archbishop in the Kulturkampf years. And he set up the St. Michael's Association, which gathered gifts for the pope across the archdiocese. His books ranged over Aristotle, Calderon, Shakespeare, and Baden history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kirkwall:
Kirkwall, from Norse Kirkjuvagr or church-bay, is the chief town of Orkney in northern Scotland and long the home of its Norse earls and bishops. Its first church honoured St. Olaf, and the landward parish still bears his name.

Earl Magnus was murdered by his cousin Haco about 1115. Magnus's nephew Ronald vowed to raise a stone minster for his uncle if he won the islands, and St. Magnus's church, begun in 1137, became cathedral of a see founded in 1102 under Trondhjem. With Glasgow, it is one of two ancient Scottish cathedrals preserved whole, 234 feet long with a 133-foot tower. Its steeple was struck by lightning in 1671, and restorations came in 1805 and 1845.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximilian-he:
Maximilian Hell, a Hungarian astronomer born at Schemnitz in 1720, died at Vienna in 1792. He joined the Society of Jesus at Trentschin in 1738 and studied philosophy at Vienna, where his early bent for science showed. In 1744 he turned to maths and astronomy as assistant to Father Joseph Franz, director of the Vienna observatory. Ordained in 1751, he taught maths at Klausenberg and in 1755 became director of the imperial observatory at Vienna.

His chief work was the yearly Ephemerides astronomicae ad meridianem Vindobonensem, begun in 1757 and packed with observations and data. The King of Denmark invited him to Vardo in Norway to watch the 1769 transit of Venus, which he did with success. He prepared his results at Copenhagen and returned to Vienna in 1770. Slow publication later raised suspicion that he had trimmed his data to match others, a charge the entry examines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-georg:
Michael George Mulhall, a statistician born in Dublin on 29 September 1829, died there on 13 December 1900. He was educated at the Irish College, Rome. Going to Buenos Aires, he founded there in 1861 the Standard, the first English paper published in South America. In 1869 he issued the Handbook of the River Plate, the first English book printed in Argentina.

His later books include the Progress of the World in 1880, the Balance Sheet of the World, 1873-1880, in 1881, and the Dictionary of Statistics in 1883. That dictionary, a standard reference few modern compilations have matched in use, was followed by the History of Prices since 1850 in 1885. In 1896 he travelled widely in Europe gathering material for an English Parliament committee reporting on a proposed Irish agriculture department. The pope decorated him for his literary work, in which his wife Marion McMurrough Mulhall, herself a prolific writer, was his active and practical helper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mother-france:
Mother Frances Mary Teresa Ball, born in Dublin on 9 January 1794, founded the Irish branch of the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary, known as the Sisters of Loreto. She died on 19 May 1861. Daughter of John Ball and Mabel Clare Bennet, she was sent at nine to the convent school at the Bar in York, run by the English Ladies of the Institute.

After her father's death in 1808 she spent time at home. In 1814, under Archbishop Daniel Murray of Dublin, she returned to York, entered the novitiate and professed in 1816 as Mary Teresa. Recalled to Dublin with two novices in 1821, she opened the order's first Irish house at Rathfarnham in 1822. She devoted her great piety and administrative skill to schools and to a sisterhood now spread across many countries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-owen-roe-o-ne:
Owen Roe O'Neill was an Irish soldier born in 1582 and dead near Cavan on 6 November 1649. He was son of Art O'Neill and nephew of Hugh, the great Earl of Tyrone. Too young for his uncle's long war, he went abroad after the peace of 1603 and served the archdukes in Flanders. By 1606 he was a captain at Brussels, and by the Thirty Years War he ranked colonel, high among Spanish commanders for skill, courage, and resource.

Chosen to hold Arras against the French in 1640, he kept the town for nearly two months with only 1,500 men. The force against him grew from 30,000 to three times that number. The French commander who took the place praised him warmly. Back in Ireland, where the flight of the earls, the Ulster plantation, and Strafford's tyranny had left Catholics no safety, O'Neill led the Catholic cause in arms until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pall: A pall is a heavy black cloth laid over the coffin in church at a funeral, or over the catafalque at other services for the departed. A white or red cross usually stands at its centre. It must always be black, though its stuff and trimming may vary. Death signs like skulls and crossbones, banned on altar and vestments, are allowed on palls. The pall is in wide use, though not prescribed, and where no bier stands, absolution needs a black cloth spread on the sanctuary floor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontius-carbo:
Pontius Carbonell was a Catalan Franciscan teacher and confessor whose identity is hard to pin down among many namesakes. He entered the Franciscan Order and lived chiefly at the Barcelona convent, where he taught and served as confessor to Saint Louis, Bishop of Toulouse, during his seven years' captivity. He died about 1320.

He was also confessor to the Infante Juan of Aragon, Archbishop of Saragossa, and probably superior in 1314. That year King James II sent him to his brother Frederick II of Sicily to beg him not to shelter the Fraticelli. He wrote commentaries on both Testaments, quoting the fathers and doctors at length, and some hold that he composed the Catena Aurea on the Gospels usually printed among Saint Thomas's works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-of-co:
Richard of Cornwall, also called Richard Rufus, was a thirteenth-century Franciscan scholar who lectured on theology at Oxford and Paris. His birth and death dates are unknown, though he was still living in 1259. He studied for a time in Paris in 1238, then returned to Oxford, and was sent with Haymo of Faversham to Rome to oppose the minister-general Elias.

By 1250 he taught the Sentences, Peter Lombard's standard theology textbook, at Oxford. Riots drove him back to Paris, where he kept lecturing and earned the title Philosophus Admirabilis, the Wonderful Philosopher. Roger Bacon, however, judged his teaching harmful, blaming it for bad effects over the next forty years. Several commentaries on the Sentences survive in manuscript under his name. A later writer denied that he was Richard Rufus at all, claiming Rufus was born at Cirencester, not Cornwall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-russe:
Richard Russell rose from humble beginnings to become a bishop in Portugal, after a youth spent in service at Lisbon College. Born in Berkshire in 1630, he became a servant at twelve to the college's newly appointed president, Dr Edward Daniel. Using his spare hours for study, he was admitted as a student five years later, then moved to Douai and Paris, where he was ordained.

Back in Lisbon as procurator in 1655, he later served as chaplain to the Portuguese ambassador in London and as secretary to the Queen of Portugal. Hopes that he might return to lead the English clergy came to nothing. Instead he accepted the see of Portalegre in 1671, reformed the diocese over ten years of hard work, and was transferred to Viseu in 1682. He spent his last eleven years there and died in 1693. His portrait survives at the English College, Lisbon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-gradwe:
Robert Gradwell was an English bishop whose career ran from revolutionary France to the rectorship of the English College at Rome. Born at Clifton-in-the-Fylde in 1777, he went to Douai in 1791. The college was suppressed by revolutionaries, and he was held for a time before returning to England in 1795. With other Douai refugees he moved to Crook Hall, Durham, where he was ordained in 1802.

For seven years he taught poetry and rhetoric at Crook Hall and the new Ushaw college. On Lingard's recommendation, Pius VII made him rector of the reopened English College at Rome in 1818, where his prudent rule made the house flourish. He also acted as Roman agent for the English vicars apostolic, and became a doctor of divinity in 1821. Consecrated Bishop of Lydda in 1828 as coadjutor for London, he died of dropsy in 1833 after years of ill health.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-catholi:
The Penal Laws began at Elizabeth's accession in 1558. Under those laws, taking Roman orders and coming to England was high treason, as were reconciliation to Rome and procuring another's. Aiding or sheltering such a priest was capital felony. Papists could not educate their children in their own religion. A home schoolmaster who skipped the parish church and lacked the bishop's licence cost parents ten pounds a month and himself forty shillings a day.

Sending children to overseas seminaries cost parents one hundred pounds and barred the children from inheriting property. Saying Mass cost 200 marks; hearing it, 100. Recusancy fines ran twenty pounds per lunar month of absence from church. In 1593 they were limited to Popish recusants. A convicted Popish recusant, besides the fine, lost office, arms, lawsuits, executorships, guardianships, and presentations. He needed a licence to travel five miles from home, and paid one hundred pounds for coming to court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-gall:
Gall was an Irish monk, one of the twelve who followed Columbanus to Gaul and settled with him at Luxeuil. He went with his master up the Rhine to Bregenz in 610. When Columbanus left for Italy in 612, Gall stayed behind in Swabia and lived as a hermit near the source of the Steinach with several companions. After his death a church rose on the spot, and before the middle of the eighth century it had grown into a monastery under its first abbot, Otmar.

The house belonged to the diocese of Constance until 818. That year Louis the Pious ranked it among the royal monasteries, and in 854 it was freed from nearly all obligation to Constance. Its name honours Gall himself, not a founder abbot. Later Lives of the saint, the oldest from the late eighth century, mix true incidents with legend, including his missionary work and the healing of Fridiburga.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-comgall:
St. Comgall was founder and abbot of the great Irish monastery at Bangor, flourishing in the sixth century. This entry follows a man of uncertain birth year, which the Irish annals place between 510 and 520. His death is put in 602 by the Annals of Tighernach and the Chronicon Scotorum, or in 597 by the Annals of Innisfallen.

He was born in Dalaradia, Ulster, near today's Magheramorne in County Antrim. He apparently served as a soldier first; freed from military service, he is said to have studied at Clonard under St. Finnian, and at Clonmacnoise under St. Ciaran, who died in 549. Next we find him in Ulster, on a Lough Erne island, with a few friends living a very severe form of monastic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ulrich-of-:
Ulrich of Zell, also called of Cluny and of Ratisbon, brought Cluniac observance to the Black Forest. Born at Ratisbon at the beginning of 1029 to the pious and rich Bernhold and Bucca, niece of Bishop Gebhard II, he was probably schooled at St Emmeram. In 1044 he went to the court of his godfather Henry IV as page to Empress Agnes.

Ordained deacon by his uncle Nidger of Freising, he became cathedral archdeacon. After a journey to Rome he gave his possessions to the poor, pilgrimaged to the Holy Land, and entered Cluny in 1061 under Hugh. There he excelled in piety and diligence, was ordained priest, and served as confessor at Marcigny and prior of its men's community. He founded Zell and died there, probably on 10 July 1093.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-and-ar:
Thomas Marshall, a controversial writer born in 1818, moved from Anglican ministry to the Catholic Church and then to public defence of Catholic schools and missions. Educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, he served as vicar of Swallowcliff before the Tractarian movement pushed him to study church government. His own research led him to leave Anglicanism, and he was received into the Catholic Church in 1845.

In 1847 he became the first inspector of Catholic schools, a post he held until a pamphlet on Anglican missions forced his resignation in 1860. After time in America he published his best known work on Christian missions in 1862 and lectured in the United States in 1870 and 1871. He died at Surbiton in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-goldwe:
Thomas Goldwell, Bishop of St. Asaph, was the last survivor of England's ancient hierarchy, dying at Rome in 1585. Born in Kent between 1501 and 1515, he studied at All Souls, Oxford, where he shone in mathematics and astronomy, and stood firm against Henry VIII's religious changes. As chaplain to Cardinal Pole he shared exile and attainder, reaching Rome in 1538.

He joined the Theatines at Naples in 1547, attended the conclave of 1549-50 with Pole, and under Mary returned as Bishop of St. Asaph. At Elizabeth's accession he fled again, refusing an Italian bishopric to work for England's conversion. He was the only English bishop at Trent, where he helped revise the Breviary and Missal and urged Elizabeth's excommunication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ulrich-zell:
Ulrich Zell was a publisher and the first printer of Cologne, born at Hanau-on-the-Main at an unknown date and dead about 1507. He learned printing before 1462 in the shop of Fust and Schöffer at Mainz. Shortly after the sack of Mainz in 1462 he moved to Cologne, whose university promised a market for printed books. He was printing there apparently as early as 1463, though his first dated book comes from 1466.

His work as printer and publisher runs to 1502, with about 120 known publications. Only nine bear his name, but he probably printed many more besides. His six kinds of type closely match the Durandus and Clement types of Fust and Schöffer, and he may even have used some of their matrices. The entry gives a compact life of a pioneer who carried the new art from Mainz to the Rhineland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-wall:
John Wall was a martyr born in Lancashire in 1620 who suffered near Worcester on 22 August 1679. Known at Douai and Rome as John Marsh, he used the mission aliases Francis Johnson, Webb, and Dormore. Son of wealthy and staunch Lancashire Catholics, he was sent very young to Douai College. He entered the Roman College on 5 November 1641, was made priest on 3 December 1645, and was sent on the mission on 12 May 1648.

On 1 January 1651 he assumed St Francis's habit at Douai's St Bonaventure Friary, and a year later professed as Joachim of St Anne. He worked as vicar and novice master at Douai until 1656, when he returned to the mission. He laboured with zeal in Worcestershire for twenty years. Seized in December 1678 at Rushock Court near Bromsgrove, he was tried for his priesthood and suffered at Worcester.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-richard-h:
Richard Hill was an English martyr executed at Durham on 27 May 1590. Very little is known of him and his fellow martyrs John Hogg and Richard Holiday. All three were Yorkshiremen: Holiday reached Reims's English College on 6 September 1584, Hill on 15 May 1587, and Hogg on 15 October 1587. All three were ordained subdeacons at Soissons, deacons and priests at Laon by Bishop Valentine Douglas.

Together with fellow martyr Edmund Duke, they left for the English mission on the following 22 March and were seized in northern England soon after landing. Arraigned, condemned, and executed at Durham under the statute 27 Elizabeth, chapter 2, they suffered with four felons who protested that they died in the same faith. Divers beholders, the entry notes, were moved by their constancy at the scaffold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-tu:
Thomas Tunstall was a northern priest executed at Norwich in July 1616. Descended from the Tunstalls of Thurland in Lancashire, he is listed in the Douai diaries under the alias Helmes and as a native of the old diocese of Carlisle. He took the college oath at Douai in 1607 and left as a priest in 1610.

Almost at once he was seized in England and spent four or five years in various prisons before escaping from Wisbech Castle. Making for a friend's house near Lynn, he was recaptured and committed to Norwich gaol, where he was tried and condemned on 12 July 1616. The holiness of his bearing on the scaffold deeply impressed onlookers. A contemporary portrait at Stonyhurst shows a still-young man with abundant black hair and a dark moustache.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-rob:
Robert Southwell was a Norfolk-born Jesuit poet executed at Tyburn in February 1595. Born at Horsham St Faith's in 1561, grandson of the courtier who had sent the poet Earl of Surrey to the block. He was raised Catholic, studied at Douai under the austere Leonard Lessius, and entered the Jesuits at Rome in 1578. Ordained in 1584, he became prefect of studies at the English College.

Sent to England in 1586 with Henry Garnet, under the name Cotton, he became chaplain to the Countess of Arundel and befriended her imprisoned husband, Philip, Earl of Arundel. His verse began in boyhood laments at his first refusal by the Society. Arrested and tortured, he was hanged at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-will:
This reference entry treats will as a topic in psychology and Catholic philosophy. Will counts as the rational appetite, set above lower drives, and its full act picks an object by the light of reason from competing aims. Its object is good in general, and its mark is freedom among different forms of good. Modern writers often stretch the word wider, covering any inner drive, even blind instinct, a usage the entry calls an abuse of terms.

Sections follow will through its links with knowledge, feeling, schooling, movement, and laboratory study. Most daily choosing, the entry notes, is swift and unreflecting, working through habit or rule of thumb rather than formal debate. Two Scholastic maxims frame the account: nothing is willed unless first known, and all knowledge starts in the senses. The piece thus maps both deliberate choice and the humbler, half-formed acts of willing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-darre:
William Darrell was an English Jesuit theologian whose Sunday reflections and conduct books reached many readers. Born in Buckinghamshire in 1651, he died at Saint Omer in 1721. From the old Catholic Darrell family of Scotney Castle, he joined the Jesuits in 1671 and made his profession in 1689. His pen defended Saint Ignatius and the Jesuits against Henry Wharton's charges in 1688 and answered Leslie's Case Stated in 1717.

Darrell's best-loved book, Moral Reflections on the Epistles and Gospels of Every Sunday, appeared in 1711 and ran through many printings. The Gentleman Instructed, on a virtuous and happy life, reached a tenth edition by 1732 and spread into Italian and Hungarian. He also issued Theses Theologicae, a treatise on the Real Presence, and a translation of discourses on Pascal's Provincial Letters. Other tracts are ascribed to him by later editors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-maxwe:
William Maxwell, fifth Earl of Nithsdale, was a Jacobite lord saved from the scaffold by his wife's daring escape plot. Born in 1676, he died at Rome in 1744. He succeeded his father at seven, and his Douglas mother raised him in Catholic faith and Stuart loyalty. About twenty-three he visited the French court to honour King James and wooed Lady Winifred Herbert, youngest daughter of the Marquis of Powis, marrying her in March 1699.

The couple lived chiefly at Terregles in Dumfriesshire and raised five children. In 1715 Nithsdale joined the rising for Prince James Stuart, was taken at Preston, and sent to the Tower under sentence of death. Lady Nithsdale begged George I in vain, then smuggled her husband out in disguise on the eve of execution. The pair fled to France and spent their last years in great poverty at Rome, attending their exiled king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-winifred-maxw:
Winifred Maxwell, Countess of Nithsdale, is famed for smuggling her husband out of the Tower on the eve of his execution. Daughter of the exiled Marquis of Powis, she died at Rome in May 1749. Her married life passed chiefly at Terregles, where news reached her of her husband's defeat at Preston. After hiding the family papers, she hurried to London to plead for him.

Winifred warned that a border Catholic with a great following and a family ever loyal to the royals could expect no mercy, and even her personal appeal to George I failed. With courage and ingenuity she then contrived his escape in women's dress on 23 February 1716 and arranged his passage to France. She returned to Scotland for papers vital to her son, endured George's charge that she had done him more mischief than any woman in Christendom, and joined her husband in Roman exile.
divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-hell:
Dante Alighieri's Hell, the Inferno, appears here in the Reverend H F Cary's blank-verse translation, the version that carried Dante to English readers for a century. It opens midway in Dante's life, lost in a gloomy wood, with Virgil offering rescue through the underworld. Thirty-four cantos descend the funnel of hell.

Dante passes the indifferent at the gate, Francesca among the lustful, gluttons, misers, heretics, and suicides turned to trees. Horned demons with great lashes drive the fraudulent along the grisly rock in the middle cantos. At the bottom, traitors lie frozen and Satan chews the worst of them. Cary's Miltonic verse keeps the journey solemn and readable.

farewell:
Farewell, by Honore de Balzac and translated by Ellen Marriage, opens with hunters joking across a stubble field. Balzac dedicates the tale to Prince Friedrich von Schwarzenberg. In the Forest of Isle-Adam, a stout marquis puffs over the furrows. His friend teases him to jump like a stag. September heat, panting dogs, and the dinner hour all feel safely ordinary.

The ordinariness is a trap. The hunt leads toward a country house. A woman lives there lost in madness, her reason gone. The narrative turns back to Napoleon's retreat from Moscow. It reaches the crossing of the Berezina river, where her mind broke. Cold, hunger, and bereavement did the work there. An old love recognizes the countess. He tries to call her back by restaging the past, scene by scene. Balzac's Adieu, as the tale is also known, studies war's aftermath. It is among his shortest and cruelest pieces.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DurhamBill_Durh:
Bill Durham wrote to Harold Weisberg on May 27, 1975 about a small object with large meaning: Lee Harvey Oswald's notebook. The letter discusses names found in it, including FBI agent James Hosty and a Gandy. A notebook page naming the agent who knew Oswald before the shooting was evidence worth arguing over.

Durham also takes up J. Edgar Hoover's notification of Robert Kennedy and claims made by former FBI agent Joseph Schott. The letter moves the way researcher mail did, lead by lead, through the open questions of the case. It preserves that exchange between two men still working the file in 1975.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MillerBill_Mill: William P. Miller filed this document in court himself, without a lawyer. He titled it 'We the People — Represent the Spirit of John F. Kennedy,' and it carries case number 112263-2000. Citizens have long filed such papers in assassination cases, asking courts to act on claims no agency would take up. The file gives Miller's title and the case number, but not the relief he asked the court to grant.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MoyersBill_Moye:
A Washington Post magazine page presents Bill Moyers in his own words and in pictures. Moyers had been President Johnson's press secretary and a central aide. One line from the page is quoted in the file: 'We won the civil rights battles of the '60s, but lost the political war.' A photograph shows Moyers with Johnson in 1964.

Moyers left the White House and became a publisher and then a television journalist. The page belongs to his years of looking back at the Johnson era he served. His quoted judgment is bleak about politics and proud about civil rights at once. The feature preserves both the man's summary of his decade and the image of him at the president's side.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaysAll_Rays_Al:
James Earl Ray signed this application for a pardon on October 6, 1980. He filed it with the Tennessee Board of Paroles. Ray was prisoner number 65477 at Brushy Mountain Prison. He was serving his sentence for the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., to which he had pleaded guilty in 1969.

Ray spent the rest of his life trying to undo that plea. He claimed he was a patsy in a larger plot and asked courts and boards, again and again, for a trial or a pardon. This application is one formal round of that campaign. It preserves his prisoner number, his prison, and his request in his own filing, twelve years after the murder.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SartorBill_Sart:
An FBI memorandum records Robert Patrick Lyons's account of meeting Bill Sartor. Lyons met Sartor through a woman named Marie Geisandorf. The meeting happened after the death of Martin Luther King Jr. Sartor was a figure whose name drew agents' attention in the King case's wide net.

Memos like this one log introductions: who met whom, through whom, and when. In a case built on possible conspiracies, introductions were evidence, the joints where a plot would have to connect. Lyons's account gives the bureau one such joint, dated after the assassination. The memorandum preserves it in the standard form, a small link kept because no one could yet say which links mattered.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Windowsill_Wind: Only a fragment of an article on the James Earl Ray case survives here. It touches on Ray's guilty plea and his later escape. The scan is garbled, and optical character reading recovers little of the text.
